metadata.title: Your Foundation Search Is Doing Market Research: How late-night shade testing helps beauty brands decide what to make next.
metadata.topic: BEAUTY & AI — WHAT A SHADE TRY-ON TELLS A BRAND
metadata.register: Warm, simple, friendly -- short sentences, no jargon; positive but fair, and clear about which numbers come from companies and which examples are illustrations, per the user's explicit tone request.
metadata.note: Sourced from the user-supplied article 'Your Foundation Search Is Doing Market Research' (pasted directly in the build request; two references: Arbelle, 'Beauty consumer trends 2026: How to win the modern beauty consumer' (Jan 19 2026), and Mani & Narayanan, 'Beauty and the (AI) beast: The makeover of personalisation, simplicity, and trust', PwC Malaysia (May 19 2026) -- see FACTCHECK.md). User asked for a 'Deep Explainer' at exactly 4:00. The toolkit's actual deep-explainer skill targets 5-10 min and requires ~20-25% of body beats to be pantry/archival stills sourced through a two-gate pipeline. Both conflict with this request: a hard 4:00 target, and the user's own note that no footage exists for this article. Built instead on the ai-explainer chassis (Claude composer cold open -> presenter intro -> body -> handoff -> outro), reusing the all-self-generated Manim/Remotion approach and af_bella/@HumanitariansAI branding used on this user's other reels. The host self-introduction ('Hi, I'm Agrima') lives in its own B00B presenter-intro beat. HEDGING (per the user's explicit request): the cosnova results (over 90% satisfaction, 20%+ add-to-cart) are labeled company-reported on screen and in narration because Arbelle sells this kind of technology; the late-night scene (B01) and the deep-shade example (B05) are labeled illustrations, not real cases; PwC's report focuses on the Asia Pacific market and the closing sources card and spoken note say so. NO real brand or company logos are used (source names appear only as plain text); faces are an abstract outline with shade swatches, no photos of real people; every visual is a generated Manim graphic. The user's explicit tone request (warm, simple, friendly; positive but fair) is a deliberate departure from this chassis's default Teardown register -- disclosed here.

props.segment: Your Foundation Search Is Doing Market Research

beats.role_note: presenter intro -- 'Hi, I'm Agrima' + lead-in; doubles as the EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY beat
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Agrima. Today: how late-night shade testing helps beauty brands decide what to make next.
beats.visual_intent: presenter card: name, then a short lead-in

beats.role_note: 11 p.m. try-on, three shades, closes the tab, buys nothing; a small clue arrived; labeled an illustration, not a real case -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: It's eleven p.m. Someone is on a makeup brand's website, phone in one hand, snack in the other. They tap try on, and test three foundation shades. One looks too pale. One looks too orange. One looks almost right. A text comes in, and they close the tab. They bought nothing, so as far as they're concerned, nothing happened. But on the brand's side, a small clue just arrived. This is an illustration, not a real case.
beats.visual_intent: illustration: a phone showing a simple face outline with three shade swatches (too pale / too orange / almost right), a text arriving, a closed tab; 11 p.m. clock, a snack; a label 'illustration -- not a real case'

beats.role_note: Arbelle: every interaction creates insight; products tried most, where customers hesitate, how personalization affects confidence to buy; behavior not just words; no review needed -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: That try-on is a quiet conversation. It helps the shopper, but it also works the other way around. Arbelle, a beauty tech company, says every interaction creates insight. Brands can see which products are tried most, where customers hesitate, and how personalization affects confidence to buy. It shows what people do, not just what they say, and it doesn't depend on anyone writing a review.
beats.visual_intent: two-way exchange: shopper and brand with arrows both ways; the brand side shows three insight rows (tried most / where they hesitate / confidence to buy); 'what people do' vs 'what they say'; source chip Arbelle, 2026

beats.act: BEAT 3 — from a tap to a product
beats.role_note: Arbelle: data guides product development, merchandising, marketing; PwC Malaysia: every interaction is a data point that improves model and product; small local trends such as glass skin in Korea, no-makeup in Japan -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: From tap to product. According to Arbelle, this data can guide three things: what to make, what to stock and show, and what to say. PwC Malaysia makes a similar point. Every interaction with AI beauty tools becomes a data point that improves the model and the product. Brands can even spot small local trends, like the glass skin look in Korea, or the no-makeup look in Japan.
beats.visual_intent: taps and swatches turning into three labels (what to make / what to stock and show / what to say); a PwC card with the two local-trend chips (glass skin -- Korea, no-makeup -- Japan)

beats.role_note: Arbelle reports cosnova: over 90% consumer satisfaction, more than 20% increase in add-to-cart rates, insights from tens of thousands of shopper sessions; company-reported because Arbelle sells this technology -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: One brand's example. Arbelle reports that cosmetics company cosnova added AI shade matching. The company says it saw over ninety percent consumer satisfaction, and an increase of more than twenty percent in add-to-cart rates. Insights came from tens of thousands of shopper sessions. But Arbelle sells this kind of technology. So these numbers are company-reported, not independent research.
beats.visual_intent: two stat cards ('over 90%' satisfaction, '20%+' add-to-cart), each labeled company-reported, plus 'tens of thousands of shopper sessions' and a note that Arbelle sells this technology; source chip

beats.act: BEAT 5 — how a gap becomes visible
beats.role_note: illustrative example (not a real case): many shoppers try the deepest shades and leave without buying; Arbelle: shoppers want to see themselves in shade ranges; PwC: narrow datasets can miss mid-to-deep tones, test across skin tones, keep humans in the loop (beauty advisors, dermatologists) -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Here's an example, not a real case. Say many shoppers keep trying the deepest foundation shades, and leave without buying. That's a hint: maybe the range has no close match. Without try-on data, the brand might never see it. Arbelle notes that shoppers want to see themselves in shade ranges. PwC warns that narrow data can make shade matchers miss mid-to-deep tones. So test across skin tones, and keep humans in the loop: beauty advisors, dermatologists. The data raises the question. A person decides.
beats.visual_intent: swatch bar of nine foundation shades light to deep with the deepest three highlighted; 'tried often -- few buy' marks labeled 'example'; then three cards: Arbelle (see themselves reflected), PwC (test across skin tones), humans in the loop; closing line

beats.role_note: PwC: recommendation data can help decide which products to keep, trim confusing long-tail items; shopper gets fewer near-duplicate shades; Arbelle: fewer returns, bigger basket, less sampling waste and over-ordering -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Back to the shelf. PwC suggests this data can help decide which products to keep. Confusing long-tail items can be trimmed, and the best products get more attention. For you, that could mean fewer near-duplicate shades, and an easier time finding yours. Arbelle adds that these tools can reduce returns, increase basket size, and cut sampling waste and over-ordering.
beats.visual_intent: a shelf of bottles with near-duplicate shades; a few fade out while the best stay highlighted; a card with three shopper benefits (fewer returns, bigger basket, less sampling waste and over-ordering)

beats.act: BEAT 7 — the part that needs care
beats.role_note: PwC: personalized beauty recommendations often rely on sensitive information (face scans, skin condition, behavior patterns); about 7 in 10 in Asia Pacific concerned; advice: collect only what's necessary, explain use, process on device when possible, clear opt-out -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: The part that needs care: a try-on uses your face. PwC notes that these recommendations often rely on sensitive information: face scans, skin condition, behavior patterns. In Asia Pacific, about seven in ten people say they're concerned about how companies collect their information. The advice: collect only what's necessary, explain what it's for, process sensitive data on the device when possible, and offer clear ways to opt out.
beats.visual_intent: a lock and a toggle; chips for face scan / skin condition / behavior patterns; ten person dots with seven filled ('about 7 in 10', Asia Pacific); four advice rows that tick on one at a time

beats.role_note: closing idea: you may have just told a brand something useful, not through a survey or a review, but by looking for the right match; a good deal for everyone -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: The next time you try on a shade and close the tab, you may have just told a brand something useful. Not through a survey or a review, just by looking for the right match. Used well, that's good for everyone. Shoppers get better matches and a wider range that includes them. Brands get a clearer idea of what to make next.
beats.visual_intent: a shopper and a small product team (abstract figures, no faces) looking at the same shade chart; two captions: better matches and a wider range / a clearer idea of what to make next

beats.role_note: Arbelle sells virtual try-on and shade-finder technology so its customer results are company-reported; PwC's report focuses on Asia Pacific; the late-night scene and deep-shade example are illustrations -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: A note on sources. Arbelle sells virtual try-on and shade-finder technology, so its customer results are company-reported. PwC's report focuses on Asia Pacific. The late-night scene and deep-shade example are illustrations.
beats.visual_intent: a sources card (two sources as plain text, no logos) with on-screen notes: company-reported; Asia Pacific focus; the late-night scene and the deep-shade example are illustrations
